client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on me all day, and I can't shake this feeling that I should be doing more to help my mom through it, but I honestly don't know what to do. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up and try, even when part of you doubts it will help — and I'm really glad you did. The grief you're carrying for your grandmother, layered with this sense of responsibility for your mom, sounds genuinely heavy, and it makes complete sense that it's sitting with you throughout the day. I'm curious — when you say you feel like you "should be doing more" for your mom, what does that voice in your head tell you that "more" would actually look like?

client: Honestly, I think the voice is saying I should be calling her every day, or going over there more, or just... knowing the right thing to say. But when I actually try to do any of that, I either freeze up or I end up saying something that feels hollow, and then I feel worse about myself for not being able to comfort her properly. It's like I have this image of what a good daughter or a good support person looks like, and I keep falling short of it.
therapist: That image of the "perfect support person" sounds like it's setting an almost impossible standard, and then when reality doesn't match it, your mind uses that gap as evidence that you're somehow failing — which is such a painful cycle to be caught in. What's worth noticing is that you *are* showing up — you're trying to call, trying to visit, trying to find words — and that effort comes from a place of genuine love, even when it feels hollow to you. I wonder, if your mom were describing you to someone else right now, what do you think she would actually say about how you've been there for her?

client: I think she'd probably say something kind, like that I've been checking in on her... but honestly, I'm not sure I fully trust that answer, because my mom tends to protect me from how she's really feeling. So even if she said something nice, I'd still have this nagging doubt that she's just saying it to make me feel better, and I wouldn't really know if I'm actually helping or just going through the motions.
therapist: It sounds like the doubt has a way of closing every door — even when you get reassurance, your mind finds a reason it doesn't count, which means you're stuck in a loop where nothing you do can ever feel like "enough." That's an exhausting place to live, and it's worth gently asking: is it possible that *certainty* you're helping isn't something you can ever fully have, and that acting from love might have to be enough even without that proof? What do you think it would feel like to let yourself off the hook, even just a little, from needing to know for sure that you're doing it "right"?

client: That idea sounds really appealing in theory, but I honestly don't know how to just decide to let myself off the hook — it's not like there's a switch I can flip. And part of me worries that if I stop holding myself to that standard, I'll just... stop trying altogether, like the guilt is the only thing keeping me showing up for her. I guess I'm not convinced that accepting uncertainty is actually a skill I can learn, rather than just something some people are naturally better at.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — it's as if your mind has convinced you that guilt is the engine keeping you going, but I'd gently invite you to consider whether it's actually love and care that's driving you, and the guilt is just the painful noise running alongside it. Tolerating uncertainty really is a skill, not a personality trait, and it's something people build gradually through small moments of practice, not a single decision. What might it look like to experiment with just one tiny act of showing up for your mom this week, and then consciously noticing what motivated you to do it — was it guilt, or was there something else there too?

client: I guess I could try that, like maybe sending her a voice message instead of a full phone call because that feels less pressure-filled. But I'm a little skeptical about the "noticing what motivated me" part, because in the moment I don't think I'll be able to separate the guilt from the love — they feel completely tangled up together, not like two distinct things I can just observe separately. I'm willing to try, but I don't want to set myself up to feel like I failed at the exercise too.
therapist: A voice message is a genuinely lovely idea, and the fact that you're already thinking about what feels manageable shows real self-awareness. You're absolutely right that guilt and love can feel completely fused together — so let's take the pressure off the "noticing" part and make it even simpler: afterward, just ask yourself one question, "did I send it?" and let that be the whole win. What do you think it would mean about you if you did send it, even while feeling uncertain and tangled up inside?

client: I think it would mean that I showed up even when I didn't feel ready or sure of myself, which... actually does feel like it matters a little when I say it out loud. But I notice I'm already bracing for the possibility that I'll send it and still feel empty afterward, like the relief won't come and I'll just be back to wondering if it was enough. I guess that's kind of what you've been pointing to this whole time, that the "enough" feeling might just never arrive the way I'm hoping it will.
therapist: What you just said — "I showed up even when I didn't feel ready" — is genuinely significant, and the fact that it landed for you, even a little, is worth holding onto. You're right that I have been gently pointing toward that, and it's meaningful that *you* arrived there yourself, because that insight will stick differently than if I'd just told you. I'm curious — if "enough" as a feeling might never fully arrive, what might it look like to start measuring your love for your mom by your actions rather than by how those actions make you feel afterward?

client: Measuring it by actions rather than feelings is an interesting way to think about it, but it also feels a little cold to me, like I'm just checking boxes rather than actually connecting with her. I think what I really want is to feel close to her through this, not just to be able to say I did the right things. I wonder if focusing too much on actions might actually make me feel more disconnected from her, not less.
therapist: That's a really important distinction, and it tells me something meaningful — what you're actually grieving here isn't just your grandmother, but also a fear of losing closeness with your mom at the very moment you both need each other most. The action-focus was never meant to replace connection, but to give you a way to keep moving toward her even when the feelings are murky — and it sounds like what you really need is permission to be *imperfect and present* with her, rather than polished and helpful. What do you think might happen if you let your mom see even a small piece of how lost and uncertain you've been feeling, rather than trying to show up as the one who has it together?

client: That actually hit me pretty hard, because I think I've been so focused on being strong for her that I haven't even considered that she might need to know I'm struggling too. But I'm scared that if I show her how lost I feel, it'll add to her burden instead of bringing us closer — like she'll feel like she has to take care of me when she's the one who just lost her mother. I don't know how to be vulnerable with her without feeling like I'm making it about myself.
therapist: The fear of burdening her is so tender and so understandable, and it actually reveals just how much you love her — but I want to gently offer another possibility: that your mom might feel *less* alone in her grief if she knew her daughter was hurting too, rather than watching you hold yourself at a careful, composed distance. There's a real difference between making it about you and letting her know you're grieving *alongside* her, and shared vulnerability can sometimes be the most genuine form of closeness there is. What do you imagine your grandmother would have wanted for the two of you, in terms of how you hold each other through this?

client: That question actually made me tear up a little, because I think my grandmother would have hated seeing us be careful and polite with each other instead of just... holding each other. She was always the one who said what was real, even when it was uncomfortable, and I think she would have wanted us to do the same. I guess I've been so afraid of doing the wrong thing that I haven't let myself just be her granddaughter grieving alongside my mom, and maybe that's what's been keeping me feeling so alone in this.
therapist: What you just touched is something really profound — you've been so focused on being a good support *for* your mom that you've been grieving alone, when the most healing thing might be to simply grieve *together*, the way your grandmother would have recognized as real. That insight didn't come from me; it came from you, and from her, in a way. I just want to sit with you in this moment for a second — how does it feel to have named that out loud?

client: It feels strange, like a relief and a sadness at the same time, because naming it makes it real in a way I wasn't quite ready for. I think part of me has been telling myself I was holding it together, and now I'm realizing I've actually just been holding it alone, which isn't the same thing at all. I'm not sure what to do with that yet, but it feels like something shifted just now, even if I can't fully explain how.
therapist: That distinction you just made — between holding it together and holding it alone — is one of the most honest and courageous things you could have said, and I think some part of you has known it for a while and finally found the words. You don't need to know what to do with it yet; sometimes a shift like this just needs to be felt before it becomes a direction. I'm wondering — when you think about talking to your mom, maybe even sending that voice message, does anything feel even slightly different now than it did when we started today?
